post_theorem_intro_text:
Note that we have assumed that $C(t)\not\equiv 0$, and so this result does not cover the results of \cite{BCFO,BCO}. However, the conditions of (b.1) are very similar to their equivalent versions in \cite{BCFO,BCO} for the case $C(t)\equiv 0$, and the general bound of (b.2.1) for the polynomial case is exactly the same. On the other hand, when we apply Darboux's Theory of Integrability in this context, because of details of the proof the bounds of (b.2.2) and (c) are less sharp than their equivalent ones in \cite{BCFO,BCO}. 

	In \cite{BCFO} using computational numerical and algebraic tools we were able to develop a method to study thoroughly the number of invariant curves that equation \eqref{Abelsinc} has, in the polynomial case. Its computational effort grows sharply as $\deg(A)$ rises though, so we only studied the cases up to $\deg(A)=5$.

	Using this method, in \cite{BCFO} for low values of $\deg(A)$ we could study the sharpness of the general bound \[\binom{\deg(A)}{(\deg(A)+1)/2}+1\] for the number of invariant curves of the equation \eqref{Abelsinc}. We did show that this bound was sharp when $\deg(A)$ was one or three, but it was not sharp when it was five. 

	On the other hand, we did not study the sharpness of the bounds provided by Darboux's Theory of Integrability when $C(t)\equiv 0$ in \cite{BCFO,BCO}, although some numerical experiments seemed to show that they were sharp for low values of $\deg(A)$. In general, the sharpness of these bounds is an open question. 

	As this paper covers the polynomial and the trigonometric case at the same time, we have decided to not develop an equivalent exhaustive method for $\eqref{ecu1}$, although we offer a lemma related with the parametrization of the equation in terms of its invariant curves, which is very helpful to make numerical experiments in this direction. Consequently, the sharpness of the bounds provided in Theorem \ref{mainth} are left as an open question. 

	The structure of the paper is as follows: first we remind the factorization properties of the ring $\mathbb{R}[\cos t,\sin t]$ and in section 2.1 we show the characterization of the invariant curves of \eqref{ecu1}; then, in section 2.2, we suppose that \eqref{ecu1} has two or more different invariant curves, and we prove (a) and (b.1); next, in section 2.3, we focus in the polynomial case to provide the general bound of (b.2.1); and finally in section 3 we apply Darboux's Theory of Integrability to prove the remaining parts of (b.2.1), together with (b.2.2) and (c).

mcq.question: Consider the differential equation \(x' = A(t)x^3 + B(t)x^2 + C(t)x\), where we are in either the polynomial case or the trigonometric case and \(\deg(\cdot)\) denotes the corresponding degree. Assume one of the following sets of hypotheses holds: (a) \(\deg(A)-\deg(C)\le 1\); (b) \(\deg(A)-\deg(C)>1\) and either we are in the polynomial case or we are in the trigonometric case with \(C(t)\) non-constant, with subcases (b.1) \(\deg(A)-\deg(C)\) is odd or \(\deg(A)+\deg(C)<2\deg(B)\), and (b.2) \(\deg(A)-\deg(C)\) is even and \(\deg(A)+\deg(C)\ge 2\deg(B)\); (c) \(\deg(A)-\deg(C)>1\) in the trigonometric case with \(C(t)\equiv c\neq 0\) constant. Which of the following is the strongest statement that can be proved about the number of invariant curves (and, where applicable, Darboux integrability or the number of rational limit cycles) of this equation?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: (a) If \(\deg(A)-\deg(C)\le 1\), then \(x' = A(t)x^3 + B(t)x^2 + C(t)x\) has at most one invariant curve. (b) If \(\deg(A)-\deg(C)>1\) and either we are in the polynomial case or we are in the trigonometric case with \(C(t)\) non-constant, then: (b.1) if \(\deg(A)-\deg(C)\) is odd or \(\deg(A)+\deg(C)<2\deg(B)\), the equation has at most two invariant curves; (b.2) if \(\deg(A)-\deg(C)\) is even and \(\deg(A)+\deg(C)\ge 2\deg(B)\), then (b.2.1) in the polynomial case the number of invariant curves is at most \(\binom{\deg(A)}{(\deg(A)+1)/2}+1\), and moreover in this case the equation is Darboux integrable if the number of invariant curves is greater than \(\deg(A)+\deg(C)+4\); (b.2.2) in the trigonometric case, an upper bound for the number of rational limit cycles is \(2\deg(A)+2\deg(C)+4\). (c) If \(\deg(A)-\deg(C)>1\) in the trigonometric case and \(C(t)\equiv c\neq 0\) is constant, then an upper bound for the number of invariant curves is \(4\deg(A)\).

theorem.content: \label{main1}  Let $B$ be a $p$-block of a solvable group $G$ with defect group $D$.  Suppose that $\varphi \in \ibr(B)$ has height zero and that $k_+(\varphi) = 0$.  If $p \geq 5$, then $D$ is abelian.  If $p = 2$, then $\mathrm {dl}(D) \leq 2$, and if $p = 3$, then $\mathrm {dl}(D) \leq 3$.
theorem.label: main1

ref_dict.orbits:
\begin{theorem}\label{orbits}  Let $G$ be a solvable group that acts faithfully and completely reducibly on a finite module $V$ of characteristic $p$.  Suppose that $$p \ndvd |G : \cent_G(v)|$$ for every $v \in V$.   Let $S$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$.  If $p \geq 5$, then $S$ is trivial.  If $p = 2$, then $S$ is abelian.  Finally, if $p=3$, then $\dl(S) \leq 2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}\label{main1}  Let $B$ be a $p$-block of a solvable group $G$ with defect group $D$.  Suppose that $\varphi \in \ibr(B)$ has height zero and that $k_+(\varphi) = 0$.  If $p \geq 5$, then $D$ is abelian.  If $p = 2$, then $\dl(D) \leq 2$, and if $p = 3$, then $\dl(D) \leq 3$.
\end{theorem}

post_theorem_intro_text:
We will in fact prove a generalization of this result, in terms of the positive height characters in $\irr(\varphi)$ - where $\varphi$ has height zero - and the derived length of the defect group of the block containing $\varphi$.  

Theorem \ref{main1} has an interesting corollary, which can be stated independently of block theory.

\begin{corollary}\label{primcor}  Let $H$ be a $p$-complement of a solvable group $G$.  Let $\alpha \in \irr(H)$ be primitive, and suppose that every constituent of $\alpha^G$ has $p'$-degree.  If $S$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$, then $S$ is abelian if $p \geq 5$.  If $p =2$, then $\mathrm {dl}(S) \leq 2$.  If $p = 3$, then $\mathrm {dl}(S) \leq 3$.
\end{corollary}

We will actually prove slightly more here as well, replacing \lq \lq $\alpha$ is primitive" with \lq \lq $\alpha$ is a Fong character".

Finally, we mention that our main tool in proving these results is the following \lq \lq large orbit" theorem, which may prove to have other applications.

\begin{theorem}\label{orbits}  Let $G$ be a solvable group that acts faithfully and completely reducibly on a finite module $V$ of characteristic $p$.  Suppose that $$p \ndvd |G : \cent_G(v)|$$ for every $v \in V$.   Let $S$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$.  If $p \geq 5$, then $S$ is trivial.  If $p = 2$, then $S$ is abelian.  Finally, if $p=3$, then $\mathrm {dl}(S) \leq 2$.
\end{theorem}

As we will see, the proof of Theorem \ref{orbits} follows easily from the work of Wolf, Gluck, and others.

The only proof-related remark is that \lq\lq the proof of Theorem~\ref{orbits} follows easily from the work of Wolf, Gluck, and others\rq\rq, but no steps are given for proving Theorem~\ref{main1}.

The explicit abc conjecture implies that (1) has only finitely many solutions $(a_1,...,a_t,n_1,n_2)\in \mathcal{N}(c)_i$. Hence the explicit abc conjecture implies that
	$$
	\prod_{i=1}^ta_i!=n_1!n_2!
	$$
	has finitely many solutions $(a_1,...,a_t,n_1,n_2)\in \mathcal{N}(c)$.

sketch:
The post-theorem discussion does not give a step-by-step proof sketch for the stated main theorem about equation (1). It only notes that “the proof of Theorem 1.1 shows that the argument can be generalized to the case where $2<s<t$,” and then sets up this generalization by assuming $n_j>a_{i_j}$ and rewriting the Diophantine equation as
\[
\prod_{i\notin\{1,i_2,\ldots,i_s\}} a_i! \,=\, \prod_{j=1}^s \Delta(m_j,k_j),
\]
with $m_j=a_{i_j}+1$ and $k_j=n_j-a_{i_j}$, introducing the parameter $k=\max\{k_2,\ldots,k_s\}$ and defining the sets $\mathcal{N}(c)_{\{i_2,\ldots,i_s\}}$ (via the constraint $k/k_1\le c$) and $\mathcal{N}(c)=\bigcup \mathcal{N}(c)_{\{i_2,\ldots,i_s\}}$. Later it only says “The proof is in fact the same as for Theorem 1.2” for a polynomial reformulation (Theorem 1.4), without outlining the argument. Thus, beyond indicating that the method of Theorem 1.1 generalizes after this simplification/reformulation, no explicit proof sketch is provided.

mcq.question:
Assume the explicit $abc$ conjecture. Consider the Diophantine equation
\[
\prod_{i=1}^t a_i! = n_1!\,n_2!
\]
in unknowns $(a_1,\ldots,a_t,n_1,n_2)$, with solutions restricted to lie in the sets $\mathcal{N}(c)_i$ (for a fixed $i$) and in $\mathcal{N}(c)$. Which of the following is the strongest consequence of these assumptions?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: Under the explicit $abc$ conjecture, the equation \(\prod_{i=1}^t a_i! = n_1!n_2!\) has only finitely many solutions \((a_1,\ldots,a_t,n_1,n_2)\in\mathcal{N}(c)_i\); consequently it has only finitely many solutions \((a_1,\ldots,a_t,n_1,n_2)\in\mathcal{N}(c)\).

choices.label: B
choices.text: Under the explicit $abc$ conjecture, for every fixed $i$ the equation \(\prod_{i=1}^t a_i! = n_1!n_2!\) has only finitely many solutions \((a_1,\ldots,a_t,n_1,n_2)\in\mathcal{N}(c)_i\); moreover, there is a constant $M=M(c,t)$ such that every such solution satisfies $\max\{a_1,\ldots,a_t,n_1,n_2\}\le M$ (hence finiteness in \(\mathcal{N}(c)\)).

choices.label: C
choices.text: Under the explicit $abc$ conjecture, for each fixed $i$ the equation \(\prod_{i=1}^t a_i! = n_1!n_2!\) has only finitely many solutions \((a_1,\ldots,a_t,n_1,n_2)\in\mathcal{N}(c)_i\).

choices.label: D
choices.text: Under the explicit $abc$ conjecture, the equation \(\prod_{i=1}^t a_i! = n_1!n_2!\) has only finitely many solutions \((a_1,\ldots,a_t,n_1,n_2)\in\mathcal{N}(c)\); in particular, for each fixed $i$ it has only finitely many solutions in \(\mathcal{N}(c)_i\).

choices.label: E
choices.text: Under the explicit $abc$ conjecture, fixing $c$ and $t$, there are only finitely many choices of the index set $\{i_2,\ldots,i_s\}$ and parameters $m_j,k_j$ with $k/k_1\le c$ for which one can rewrite a solution of \(\prod_{i=1}^t a_i! = n_1!n_2!\) in the form \[\prod_{i\notin\{1,i_2,\ldots,i_s\}} a_i! \,=\, \prod_{j=1}^s \Delta(m_j,k_j),\] and hence there are only finitely many solutions in each \(\mathcal{N}(c)_i\) and in \(\mathcal{N}(c)\).

theorem.content:
\label{thm:general}
    Let $\beta$ be an algebraic number with $|\beta|=1$ which is not a root of unity. Then $\frac{\operatorname{Arg}(\beta)}{2\pi} \in \left(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}\right]$ is a Diophantine number.
theorem.label: thm:general

post_theorem_intro_text:
By applying the previous result to the solutions of equation \eqref{eq:main}, together with the classical theorems described in Section \ref{sec:pre}, we obtain the following arithmetic statements.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:3props}
    Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer and let $\alpha \in \left( 0, \frac{\pi}{2} \right)$ be a solution of \eqref{eq:main}. Then the following statements hold.
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
        \item $\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}$ is a Diophantine number.
        \item $\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}$ is transcendental.
        \item $\alpha$ is transcendental.
    \end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

We observe that items $(a)$ and $(b)$ of the previous theorem extend the result of Cyr~\cite{Cyr2012}, while item $(c)$ provides the transcendence of the solution $\alpha$ itself.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section \ref{sec:pre}, we introduce the main tools used in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:general}, including several algebraic ingredients, as well as the Baker-Wüstholz Theorem, which provides a lower bound for a non-zero linear forms in logarithms, the Gelfond-Schneider Theorem and the Hermite-Lindemann Theorem, which are two remarkable results in transcendence theory. Section \ref{sec:proof} contains the proof of the main result (Theorem \ref{thm:general}). In Section \ref{sec:eqtan}, we apply the main result, together with the remarkable theorems presented in Section \ref{sec:pre}, to the solutions of equation \eqref{eq:main} in order to prove Theorem \ref{thm:3props}. Finally, in Section \ref{sec:conclusion}, we summarize the results obtained in this paper and present an open problem.

Which of the following is the strongest statement that can be proved about $\frac{\operatorname{Arg}(\beta)}{2\pi}$ under these assumptions?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: The number $\frac{\operatorname{Arg}(\beta)}{2\pi}\in\left(-\frac12,\frac12\right]$ is a Diophantine number.

choices.label: B

choices.label: D

choices.label: E

\section{Inequalities for Riesz potentials}
\label{appB}

In this section, we include some inequalities for Riesz potentials which were used for the proof of the QCLT in the case when $\k$ is the Riesz kernel.

We recall that the Riesz kernel of order $\alpha \in (0,d)$ is defined by 
\[
R_{d,\alpha}(x)=C_{d,\alpha}|x|^{-(d-\alpha)} \quad \mbox{with} \quad C_{d,\alpha}=\pi^{-\frac{d}{2}}2^{-\alpha} \frac{\Gamma(\frac{d-\alpha}{2})}{\Gamma(\frac{\alpha}{2})}.
\]
Its Fourier transform (in the sense of distributions) is $\cF R_{d,\alpha}(\xi)=|\xi|^{-\alpha}$, since
\[
\int_{\bR^d}\varphi(x)|x|^{-\alpha}dx=C_{d,\alpha} \int_{\bR^d}\cF \varphi(\xi)|\xi|^{-(d-\alpha)}d\xi \quad 
\mbox{for any $\varphi \in \cS(\bR^d)$},
\]
where $\cS(\bR^d)$ is the set of rapidly decreasing functions on $\bR^d$.

\medskip

For the next result, we refer to Theorem 1, p.119 of \cite{stein70}.

\begin{theorem}[Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolov inequality]
\label{HLS}
For any $\alpha \in (0,d)$ and $p>\frac{d}{d-\alpha}$, 
\[
\| \varphi *R_{d,\alpha}\|_{L^p(\bR^d)} \leq A_{d.\alpha,p}\|\varphi\|_{L^{q}(\bR^d)} \quad \mbox{for any $\varphi \in L^q(\bR^d)$},
\]
where $A_{d,\alpha,p}>0$ is a constant depending on $(d,\alpha,p)$, and $q$ is defined by:
\[
\frac{1}{q}=\frac{1}{p}+\frac{\alpha}{d}.
\]
(Condition $p>\frac{d}{d-\alpha}$ is equivalent to $q>1$.)
\end{theorem}

As a consequence of Theorem \ref{HLS}, we obtain the following lemma.

\begin{lemma}
\label{Hol-HLS}
For any $\alpha \in (0,d)$, $q \in (1,\frac{d}{\alpha})$, $\varphi \in L^q(\bR^d)$ and $\psi \in L^{q'}(\bR^d)$,
\[
\left|\int_{\bR^d}\int_{\bR^d}\varphi(x)\psi(y) R_{d,\alpha}(x-y) dxdy \right| \leq A_{d,\alpha,p} \|\varphi\|_{L^q(\bR^d)} \|\psi\|_{L^{q'}(\bR^d)},
\]
where $A_{d,\alpha,p}$ is the constant  from Theorem \ref{HLS}, and $(p,q')$ are defined by
\[
\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=1 \quad \mbox{and} \quad \frac{1}{q}+\frac{1}{q'}=1+\frac{\alpha}{d}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We apply H\"older's inequality, letting $\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=1$, and obtain that
\begin{align*}
\left|\int_{\bR^d}\int_{\bR^d}\varphi(x)\psi(y) R_{d,\alpha}(x-y) dxdy \right|
& =\left| \int_{\bR^d}\varphi(x) \big(\psi * R_{d,\alpha} \big) dx\right| \leq \|\varphi\|_{L^q(\bR^d)} \|\psi * R_{d,\alpha}\|_{L^p(\bR^d)}.
\end{align*}
Note that $q<\frac{d}{\alpha}$ is equivalent to $p>\frac{d}{d-\alpha}$.
Therefore, by Theorem \ref{HLS} 
\[
 \|\psi * R_{d,\alpha}\|_{L^p(\bR^d)} \leq A_{d,\alpha,p}  \|\psi \|_{L^{q'}(\bR^d)},
\]
where $\frac{1}{q'}=\frac{1}{p}+\frac{\alpha}{d}$. Finally, we note that $
1-\frac{1}{q}=\frac{1}{p}=\frac{1}{q'}-\frac{\alpha}{d}$, and hence, $\frac{1}{q}+\frac{1}{q'}=1+\frac{\alpha}{d}$.

\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Functional Central Limit Theorem]
\label{FCLT}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem \ref{QCLT}, for any $R>0$,
the process $\{F_R(t)\}_{t\geq 0}$ has a $\gamma$-H\"older continuous modification (denoted also $F_R$), for any $\gamma \in (0,\frac{\beta}{2})$, where $\beta$ is given by \eqref{def-beta}.
Moreover,
\[
\frac{1}{R^{\beta/2}}F_R(\cdot) \stackrel{d}{\to} \cG(\cdot) \quad \mbox{in $C[0,\infty)$ as $R \to \infty$},
\]
where $\{\cG(t)\}_{t\geq 0}$ is a zero-mean Gaussian process with covariance 
$\bE[\cG(t) \cG(s)]=K(t,s)$, and $K(t,s)$ given by Theorem \ref{cov-th}. Here $\stackrel{d}{\to}$ denotes the convergence in distribution, and $C[0,\infty)$ is equipped with the uniform convergence on compact sets.
\end{theorem}

post_theorem_intro_text:
\noindent
We say that the even log-concave measure $\mu$ satisfies the strong dimensional Brunn--Minkowski condition if \eqref{eq:strong_dim_BM} holds for every origin-symmetric $K$ of class $C^2_+$. The fact that this condition implies the dimensional Brunn--Minkowski conjecture \eqref{eq:dim_BM} follows immediately from an integration by parts, together with the symmetry of the problem. See Corollary \ref{cor:strong_then_dim} later.

To state our second result, we introduce some additional notation. Given $u$ and $\mu$ as in Theorem \ref{thm:main_1}, for every $\psi \in C^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ we define the $\mu$-weighted Laplacian as $\Lmalaka_\mu(\psi)=\Delta \psi-\langle \nabla u, \nabla \psi \rangle$. Moreover, we say that a measure $\eta$ is log-concave with respect to $\mu$ if $\eta$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$ and its corresponding density  $\, \mathrm{d} \eta / \, \mathrm{d} \mu$ is a log-concave function. The notion of hereditary convexity put forth in \cite{ cordero2025concavity}, inspired by \cite{Kol_Liv_Gardner-Zvavitch} in the particular case of log-concave measures, is defined as follows. A log-concave measure $\mu$ is hereditarily convex if it is even, and for every even measure $\eta$ which is log-concave with respect to $\mu$ and every even $\psi$ such that $\Lmalaka_\mu(\psi) \in L_2(\eta)$, one has 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hered_conv}
    \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} ||\nabla^2 \psi||^2_{\rm HS}+\langle \nabla^2 u \nabla \psi, \nabla \psi \rangle \, \mathrm{d} \eta \geq \frac{\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \Lmalaka_\mu(\psi)\, \mathrm{d} \eta\right)^2}{\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \Lmalaka_\mu\left(\frac{|x|^2}{2}\right) \, \mathrm{d} \eta}.
\end{equation}
Here, $||\cdot||_{\rm HS}$ denotes the Hilbert--Schmidt norm of matrices, and $|x|^2=\langle x, x \rangle$. Our second result reads as follows.
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main_2}
    Consider $\mu$ as in Theorem \ref{thm:main_1}. If $\mu$ is hereditarily convex, then $\mu$ satisfies the strong dimensional Brunn--Minkowski condition.
\end{theorem}\noindent
We shall prove, in fact, that the strong dimensional Brunn--Minkowski condition follows when $\mu$ is hereditarily convex only with respect to uniform measures on non-empty compact and convex subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$. 

\medskip

To summarize this note, the results presented above show that if $\mu$ is an even-log concave measure as in Theorem \ref{thm:main_1}, the implications in \cite[(62)]{cordero2025concavity} can be refined as follows:
\begin{eqnarray}\notag
 & &    \textrm{$\mu$ verifies \eqref{eq:dim_BM}} \notag \\
 & \rotatebox[origin=c]{45}{\(\Longrightarrow\)} &  \notag\\ \notag
 \textrm{$\mu$ is hereditarily convex} \Rightarrow \textrm{$\mu$ satisfies the strong dim-BM condition}  & &  \\
 & \rotatebox[origin=c]{315}{\(\Longrightarrow\)}  & \notag \\
 & &  \textrm{$\mu$ verifies \eqref{eq:B_conj}}. \notag
\end{eqnarray}

No proof sketch is provided there for the log-concavity conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:main_1} itself.

Let $u \in C^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ be an even convex function such that its Hessian matrix $
abla^2 u$ is positive definite, and let $\mu$ be the associated log-concave measure with density $d\mu(x)=e^{-u(x)}\,dx$. Let $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a convex, compact set of class $C^2_+$, with support function $h_K$ and outer unit normal $
u_K$ on $\partial K$. Assume that
$$ rac{\mu(K)}{\int_{\partial K} h_K(
u_K)\, d\mu} \le p(\mu,K).$$
(Here $e^tK:=\{e^t x: x\in K\}$.) What is the strongest statement that can be proved about the map $t\mapsto \mu(e^t K)$ for $t\in\mathbb{R}$ (and, if the same inequality holds for every such $K$, about $\mu$)?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: The function $t\mapsto \mu(e^t K)$ is log-concave on $\mathbb{R}$. Moreover, if the inequality $\frac{\mu(K)}{\int_{\partial K} h_K(\nu_K)\, d\mu} \le p(\mu,K)$ holds for every convex, compact $C^2_+$ set $K$, then $\mu$ satisfies conjecture (B), i.e. for every such $K$ the map $t\mapsto \mu(e^t K)$ is log-concave on $\mathbb{R}$.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The function $t\mapsto \mu(e^tK)$ is \emph{concave} on $\mathbb{R}$. Moreover, if the inequality $\frac{\mu(K)}{\int_{\partial K} h_K(\nu_K)\,d\mu}\le p(\mu,K)$ holds for every convex, compact $C^2_+$ set $K$, then for all such $K$ the map $t\mapsto \mu(e^tK)$ is concave on $\mathbb{R}$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The function $t\mapsto \mu(e^tK)$ is log-concave on a neighborhood of $t=0$ (equivalently, $\log \mu(e^tK)$ is concave for $|t|$ sufficiently small, depending on $\mu$ and $K$). Moreover, if the same inequality holds for every convex, compact $C^2_+$ set $K$, then this local log-concavity near $t=0$ holds for every such $K$.

choices.label: D
choices.text:
The function $t\mapsto \mu(e^tK)$ is log-concave on $[0,\infty)$. Moreover, if the inequality $\frac{\mu(K)}{\int_{\partial K} h_K(\nu_K)\,d\mu}\le p(\mu,K)$ holds for every convex, compact $C^2_+$ set $K$, then $\mu$ satisfies conjecture \emph{(dim-BM)}, i.e. for all convex, compact $C^2_+$ sets $K,L$ and all $t\in[0,1]$ one has
\[
\mu((1-t)K+tL)^{\frac1n}\ge (1-t)\mu(K)^{\frac1n}+t\mu(L)^{\frac1n}.
\]

choices.label: E
choices.text:
The function $t\mapsto \mu(e^tK)$ is log-concave on $\mathbb{R}$, and if the inequality $\frac{\mu(K)}{\int_{\partial K} h_K(\nu_K)\,d\mu}\le p(\mu,K)$ holds for every convex, compact $C^2_+$ set $K$, then $\mu$ satisfies the full dimensional Brunn--Minkowski inequality
\[
\mu((1-t)K+tL)^{\frac1n}\ge (1-t)\mu(K)^{\frac1n}+t\mu(L)^{\frac1n}
\]
for all convex compact $K,L$ (with no $C^2_+$ regularity assumed).

mcq.question: Let \(\theta_1,\theta_2,p\) be integers such that \(\gcd(\theta_1,p)=\gcd(\theta_2,p)=1\). Assume further that \(\theta_1\equiv \theta_2\pmod p\). What is the strongest statement that can be proved about the values of \(\zeta_p(\theta_1)\) and \(\zeta_p(\theta_2)\)?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: Under these assumptions, \(\zeta_p(\theta_1)=\zeta_p(\theta_2)\).

choices.label: B
choices.text: Under these assumptions, one can conclude only that \(\zeta_p(\theta_1)^3=\zeta_p(\theta_2)^3\) (equivalently, \(\chi_p(\theta_1)=\chi_p(\theta_2)\)), but not necessarily that \(\zeta_p(\theta_1)=\zeta_p(\theta_2)\).

choices.label: C
choices.text: Under these assumptions, \(\zeta_p(\theta_1)=\zeta_p(\theta_2)\) holds whenever \(\zeta_p(\theta)=\frac{1+\chi_p(\theta)}{2}\) for some \(\chi_p:\{\xi\in\mathbb Z:\gcd(\xi,p)=1\}\to\{-1,1\}\) that depends only on the residue class of \(\theta\bmod p\) (e.g., the Legendre symbol).

choices.label: D
choices.text: Under these assumptions, \(\zeta_p(\theta_1)=\zeta_p(\theta_2)\) holds only in the case \(\theta_1\equiv \theta_2\pmod{p^2}\); congruence modulo \(p\) is in general insufficient to force equality of \(\zeta_p\)-values.

choices.label: E

ref_dict.KT:
\begin{Proposition}[Katz]\label{KT}
Let $\chi$ be a non-trivial multiplicative character of $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$ and let
$g\in\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$ generate the extension
$\mathbb{F}_{p^n}=\mathbb{F}_p(g)$. Then, for any interval
$I\subseteq [1,p]\cap\mathbb{Z}$,
\[
\left|\sum_{t\in I}\chi(g+t)\right|
\le c(n)\sqrt{p}\log p .
\]
\end{Proposition}

post_theorem_intro_text:
While this theorem provides strong cancellation, it requires each interval to be of Burgess length, precluding situations in which some intervals are short while others are long. This limitation was partially overcome by M. R. Gabdullin \cite{GB}, who generalized Konyagin's result for $n=2,3$ under a weaker product condition.

\begin{theorem}[Gabdullin \cite{GB}]
Let $n\in\{2,3\}$, let $\chi$ be a nontrivial multiplicative character of $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$, and suppose
\[
|B|\geq p^{n(1/4+\varepsilon)}, \qquad H_1\leq H_2\leq\cdots\leq H_n.
\]
Then
\[
\left|\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in B}\chi(\mathbf{x})\right|
\ll_{n,\varepsilon} |B| p^{-\varepsilon^2/12}.
\]
\end{theorem}

In this paper, we generalize Gabdullin's result to arbitrary dimension $n$. Our main theorem establishes nontrivial cancellation for character sums over general boxes in $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$, assuming only a lower bound on the volume of the box.

\begin{theorem}[Main Theorem]\label{MT}
Let $n\geq2$, let $\chi$ be a nontrivial multiplicative character of $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$, and suppose
\[
|B|\geq p^{n(1/4+\varepsilon)},\qquad
H_1\leq H_2\leq\cdots\leq H_n\leq \sqrt{p/2}.
\]
Then
\[
\left|\sum_{x\in B}\chi(x)\right|
\ll |B|\, p^{-\varepsilon^2
\frac{1-\frac{1}{2n}}{\left(1+\frac{1}{4n}\right)\left(2-\frac{1}{2n}\right)}}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}
If the extension degree $n$ is prime, the monotonicity assumption $H_1\leq\cdots\leq H_n\leq \sqrt{p/2}$ may be removed. A sketch of the argument is given in Case 3 of the proof of Theorem \ref{MT}.
\end{remark}

In a previous work \cite{Ch}, the author studied character sums over sublattices of codimension one in $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$, obtaining nontrivial bounds under significantly weaker length conditions.

\begin{theorem}[Chattopadhyay \cite{Ch}]
Let $\chi$ be a nontrivial multiplicative character of $\mathbb{F}_{p^d}$, and let $\omega$ be a generator of $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}^\ast$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta(\varepsilon)>0$ such that if $I_0,\ldots,I_{n-2}$ are intervals of length $p^{\rho''_n+\varepsilon}$, where
\[
\rho''_n=\frac{1460-1000n+\sqrt{1000000n^2-1960000n+490000}}{960},
\]
then
\[
\sum_{x_0\in I_0,\ldots,x_{n-2}\in I_{n-2}}
\chi(x_0+x_1\omega+\cdots+x_{n-2}\omega^{n-2})
\ll p^{-\delta(\varepsilon)} |I_0|\cdots|I_{n-2}|.
\]
\end{theorem}

The novelty of this result lied in treating character sums over sublattices of codimension one.

\medskip

As a consequence of our Main Theorem, we can now treat sublattices of co-dimension at least $o(n)$, while allowing each interval to have length as small as $p^{1/4+\varepsilon}$. Moreover, we are no longer restricted to a special choice of basis; the result holds for an arbitrary basis of $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$, in contrast with our previous work.
\begin{Corollary}
Let $\chi$ be a nontrivial multiplicative character of $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$, let $I_i \subset \mathbb{Z}$ be intervals of lengths $H_i$, and let $\{\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_n\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$. 
For every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta(\varepsilon)>0$ such that
\[
\left|\sum_{x_1\in I_1,\ldots,x_k\in I_k}
\chi(x_1\omega_1+\cdots+x_k\omega_k)\right|
\ll_{n,\varepsilon}
H_1\cdots H_k\,p^{-\delta(\varepsilon)},
\]
provided that
\[
H_i \ge p^{\frac{n}{k}\left(\frac14+\varepsilon\right)}
\quad (1\le i\le k),
\]
where
\[
\delta(\varepsilon)
=
\varepsilon^2
\frac{1-\frac{1}{2n}}{\left(1+\frac{1}{4n}\right)\left(2-\frac{1}{2n}\right)}.
\]
In particular, if $k=n-o(n)$, then the condition becomes
$H_i\geq p^{\frac{n}{n-o(n)}(1/4+\varepsilon)}$, and this exponent tends to $1/4+\varepsilon$ as $n\to\infty$. Thus, in the limit of large dimension, we obtain Burgess-strength bounds in each coordinate.
\end{Corollary}

\medskip

The proof of the Main Theorem closely follows the approach of \cite{GB}, employing techniques from \cite{C1}, \cite{K} and \cite{Kon} to estimate character sums over boxes in finite fields whose side lengths are at most $\sqrt{p/2}$. Our argument begins with the classical additive shifting technique $x\mapsto x+yz$ introduced by Burgess \cite{B2}. Applying H\"older's inequality twice to the resulting sum of shifted characters produces three terms: one is related to the multiplicative energy of the box, while the remaining terms can be bounded using Weil's bound and trivial estimates. Consequently, achieving a nontrivial saving for the character sum reduces to obtaining a bound on the multiplicative energy of a set in $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$ which are described in Lemma \ref{l1} and Lemma \ref{l2}. More specifically, we employ tools from the geometry of numbers, in particular the concepts of successive minima and Minkowski's second theorem, together with an auxiliary lemma that provides upper and lower bounds for the product of successive minimas which turns out to be an essential ingredient in our energy estimate.\\

In fact, we have also removed the boundedness assumption on the side lengths of the boxes in Theorem~\ref{MT}, as described in \textbf{Remark~1}, when the degree of the extension is prime. The key ingredient in the proof of \textbf{Remark~1} is Theorem~\ref{KT}, which provides square-root cancellation for the corresponding complete character sum over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$. Under the remaining assumption that the larger side length of the box exceeds $p^{1/2+\varepsilon}$, we obtain a non-trivial saving for the character sum along that direction. Estimating the remaining summations trivially then yields an overall non-trivial saving over the volume of the box. For further details, see \textbf{Case~3} in the proof of the main theorem. 

\medskip

{\bf Acknowledgments.} The author expresses his sincere gratitude to Professor Stephan Baier for his valuable conversations. The author thanks the Ramakrishna Mission Vivekananda Educational and Research Institute for an excellent work environment. The research of the author was supported by a CSIR Ph.D. fellowship under file number 09/0934(13170)/2022-EMR-I.

mcq.question:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $\varepsilon>0$. Let $B$ be an $n$-dimensional box (with side lengths $H_1,\dots,H_n$) and let $\chi(\mathbf{x})$ be a character evaluated on points $\mathbf{x}\in B$. Assume that
\[
H_i>p^{1/4+\varepsilon}\quad\text{for all }1\le i\le n.
\]
What is the strongest statement that can be proved about the magnitude of the character sum $\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in B}\chi(\mathbf{x})$ under these assumptions?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text:
One has the bound
\[
\left|\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in B}\chi(\mathbf{x})\right|\ll_{n,\varepsilon} p^{-\varepsilon^2/2}\,|B|.
\]

choices.label: B
choices.text:
One has the bound
\[
\left|\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in B}\chi(\mathbf{x})\right|\ll_{n,\varepsilon} p^{-\varepsilon^2/2}\,\prod_{i=1}^n H_i.
\]
(in particular, this holds without any further restriction such as $H_i\le \sqrt{p/2}$).

choices.label: C
choices.text:
One has a nontrivial saving over the trivial bound, i.e.
\[
\left|\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in B}\chi(\mathbf{x})\right|\ll_{n,\varepsilon} |B|\,p^{-c(\varepsilon)}
\]
for some constant $c(\varepsilon)>0$ depending only on $\varepsilon$ (and $n$).

choices.label: D
choices.text:
One has square-root cancellation in terms of the volume:
\[
\left|\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in B}\chi(\mathbf{x})\right|\ll_{n,\varepsilon} p^{-\varepsilon^2/2}\,|B|^{1/2}.
\]

choices.label: E
choices.text:
One has the stronger saving
\[
\left|\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in B}\chi(\mathbf{x})\right|\ll_{n,\varepsilon} p^{-\varepsilon/2}\,|B|,

whenever $H_i>p^{1/4+\varepsilon}$ for all $1\le i\le n$.

theorem.content:
[Graph currents satisfy the section constraint]\label{lem:graph-sectionconstraint}
Let $V$ be a smooth unit vector field on $\mathbb S^n$ and let $s_V\colon \mathbb S^n\to E=\mathrm{UT}\Sph^n$ be the associated section $s_V(x)=(x,V(x))$.
Define the graph current $T\Gamma_V:=(s_V)_\#\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket$.
Then $T\Gamma_V\in\mathbf I_n(E)$, $\partial T\Gamma_V=0$, and
\[
\pi_\#T\Gamma_V=\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket.
\]
In particular, $T\Gamma_V\in\mathcal S$.
theorem.label: lem:graph-sectionconstraint

ref_dict.prop:Tp:
\begin{proposition}[Pole behavior in $E$: boundary of the radial graph current]\label{prop:Tp}
Fix $p\in\Sph^n$ and set $r=\dist(\cdot,p)$.  Let $R=\nabla r$ on $\Sph^n\setminus\{\pm p\}$ and consider the graph map
\[
s_R\colon \Sph^n\setminus\{\pm p\}\to E,\qquad s_R(x)=(x,R(x)).
\]
Let $T_p$ denote the associated integral $n$--current in $E$, i.e.\ the current of integration over the embedded graph $s_R(\Sph^n\setminus\{\pm p\})$ with the orientation induced from $\Sph^n$.
Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item $T_p$ has finite mass, $\pi_\#T_p=\llbracket \Sph^n\rrbracket$, and $T_p$ is $\omega$--calibrated at $|T_p|$--a.e.\ point.  In particular,
\[
\mass(T_p)=T_p(\omega)=\pi\,\vol(\Sph^{d})=c(m;1)\,\vol(\Sph^n).
\]
\item Let $\iota_q\colon \Sph^{d}\to E$ be the fiber inclusion $\iota_q(v)=(q,v)$ and denote the oriented fiber currents by $F_q:=(\iota_q)_\push\llbracket \Sph^{d}\rrbracket$.
Then
\[
\partial T_p = -\bigl(F_p + F_{-p}\bigr).
\]
In particular, $T_p$ is \emph{not} an $n$--cycle in $E$ (it represents a relative class in $H_n(E,\,\pi^{-1}(p)\cup\pi^{-1}(-p))$).
\item The support of $T_p$ contains the full fibers $\pi^{-1}(\pm p)$.  However, $|T_p|$ assigns those fibers zero $n$--dimensional mass.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
ref_dict.def:Jn:
\begin{definition}[$n$--Jacobian of a linear map]\label{def:Jn}
Let $L:V\to W$ be a linear map between Euclidean inner-product spaces and let $P\subset V$ be an
$n$--dimensional subspace.
We define the \emph{$n$--Jacobian} of $L$ restricted to $P$ by
\[
J_n(L|_P):=\bigl|\wedge^n(L|_P)\bigr|
=\sqrt{\det\bigl((L|_P)^{*}(L|_P)\bigr)}.
\]
Equivalently, if $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ is an orthonormal basis of $P$, then
$J_n(L|_P)=|Le_1\wedge\cdots\wedge Le_n|$.
In particular, $J_n(L|_P)>0$ if and only if $L|_P:P\to W$ has rank $n$ (equivalently, is an
isomorphism onto its image).
\end{definition}

post_theorem_intro_text:
\begin{proof}
Since $\pi\circ s_V=\mathrm{Id}_{\mathbb S^n}$, the map $s_V$ is smooth and proper (because $\mathbb S^n$ is compact).
Moreover $s_V$ is an embedding, with inverse $\pi\vert_{\Gamma_V}$ on its image $\Gamma_V:=s_V(\mathbb S^n)$.
We orient $\Gamma_V$ by pushforward of the given orientation on $\mathbb S^n$.

The current $T\Gamma_V=(s_V)_\#\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket$ is therefore the integration current $\llbracket \Gamma_V\rrbracket$ on the smooth oriented submanifold $\Gamma_V$, hence $T\Gamma_V\in\mathbf I_n(E)$.
Because $\partial\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket=0$ and pullback commutes with $\mathrm d$, for every $\psi\in\Omega^{n-1}(E)$ we have
\[
(\partial T\Gamma_V)(\psi)=T\Gamma_V(\mathrm d\psi)
=\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket\bigl(s_V^*(\mathrm d\psi)\bigr)
=\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket\bigl(\mathrm d(s_V^*\psi)\bigr)
=(\partial\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket)(s_V^*\psi)=0,
\]
so $\partial T\Gamma_V=0$.

Finally, for any $\eta\in\Omega^n(\mathbb S^n)$, using the definition of pushforward,
\[
(\pi_\#T\Gamma_V)(\eta)=T\Gamma_V(\pi^*\eta)
=\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket\bigl(s_V^*(\pi^*\eta)\bigr)
=\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket\bigl((\pi\circ s_V)^*\eta\bigr)
=\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket(\eta).
\]
Thus $\pi_\#T\Gamma_V=\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket$, as claimed.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[$n$--Jacobian of a linear map]\label{def:Jn}
Let $L:V\to W$ be a linear map between Euclidean inner-product spaces and let $P\subset V$ be an
$n$--dimensional subspace.
We define the \emph{$n$--Jacobian} of $L$ restricted to $P$ by
\[
J_n(L|_P):=\bigl|\wedge^n(L|_P)\bigr|
=\sqrt{\det\bigl((L|_P)^{*}(L|_P)\bigr)}.
\]
Equivalently, if $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ is an orthonormal basis of $P$, then
$J_n(L|_P)=|Le_1\wedge\cdots\wedge Le_n|$.
In particular, $J_n(L|_P)>0$ if and only if $L|_P:P\to W$ has rank $n$ (equivalently, is an
isomorphism onto its image).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Rectifiable sections and multiplicity-one]\label{def:rectifiable-section}
Let $E=\mathrm{UT}\Sph^n$ with projection $\pi:E\to\mathbb S^n$.
An integer rectifiable $n$--current $T=\llbracket \mathcal N,\theta,\tau\rrbracket\in\mathbf I_n(E)$ is called a \emph{rectifiable section a.e.} if
\[
J_n\bigl(\mathrm d\pi_y\vert_{\operatorname{Tan}(T,y)}\bigr)>0\qquad\text{for }|T|\text{--a.e. }y\in\mathcal N,
\]
Here $J_n$ denotes the $n$--Jacobian as in Definition~\ref{def:Jn}.  Equivalently, if $\mathrm d\pi_y\vert_{\operatorname{Tan}(T,y)}: \operatorname{Tan}(T,y)\to T_{\pi(y)}\mathbb S^n$ is an isomorphism for $|T|$--a.e. $y$.
We call $T$ \emph{multiplicity-one} if for $\mathcal H^n$--a.e. $x\in\mathbb S^n$ the fiber intersection $\mathcal N\cap\pi^{-1}(x)$ consists of a single point $(x,V(x))$ and $\theta(x,V(x))=1$.
\end{definition}

Finally, we record that the canonical two-pole radial graph current associated to $\nabla\operatorname{dist}(\cdot,p)$ is \emph{not} a cycle:
its boundary is supported on the two pole fibers and is nonzero (see Proposition~\ref{prop:Tp} for the explicit oriented boundary formula).

Since $\pi\circ s_V=\mathrm{Id}_{\mathbb S^n}$, the map $s_V$ is smooth and proper (as $\mathbb S^n$ is compact), and is an embedding with inverse $\pi\vert_{\Gamma_V}$ on $\Gamma_V:=s_V(\mathbb S^n)$. Orient $\Gamma_V$ by pushforward of the given orientation on $\mathbb S^n$. Then $T\Gamma_V=(s_V)_\#\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket$ is the integration current $\llbracket \Gamma_V\rrbracket$ on the smooth oriented submanifold $\Gamma_V$, hence $T\Gamma_V\in\mathbf I_n(E)$. For the boundary, use $\partial\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket=0$ and that pullback commutes with $\mathrm d$: for every $\psi\in\Omega^{n-1}(E)$,
\[
(\partial T\Gamma_V)(\psi)=T\Gamma_V(\mathrm d\psi)=\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket\bigl(\mathrm d(s_V^*\psi)\bigr)=(\partial\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket)(s_V^*\psi)=0,
\]
so $\partial T\Gamma_V=0$. Finally, to compute the projection, for any $\eta\in\Omega^n(\mathbb S^n)$ use the definition of pushforward:
\[
(\pi_\#T\Gamma_V)(\eta)=T\Gamma_V(\pi^*\eta)=\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket\bigl((\pi\circ s_V)^*\eta\bigr)=\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket(\eta),
\]
thus $\pi_\#T\Gamma_V=\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket$ (and hence $T\Gamma_V\in\mathcal S$).

expanded_theorem:
[Graph currents satisfy the section constraint]\label{lem:graph-sectionconstraint}
Let $V$ be a smooth unit vector field on $\mathbb S^n$ and let $s_V\colon \mathbb S^n\to E=\mathrm{UT}\Sph^n$ be the associated section $s_V(x)=(x,V(x))$.
Define the graph current $T\Gamma_V:=(s_V)_\#\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket$.
Then $T\Gamma_V\in\mathbf I_n(E)$, $\partial T\Gamma_V=0$, and
\[
\pi_\#T\Gamma_V=\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket.
\]
In particular, $T\Gamma_V\in\mathcal S\,.$

mcq.question: Let $V$ be a smooth unit vector field on $\mathbb S^n$, let $E=\mathrm{UT}\,\mathbb S^n$ with bundle projection $\pi\colon E\to\mathbb S^n$, and let $s_V\colon \mathbb S^n\to E$ be the associated section $s_V(x)=(x,V(x))$. Define the graph current $T\Gamma_V:=(s_V)_\#\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket$. What is the strongest statement that can be proved about $T\Gamma_V$ under these assumptions?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: $T\Gamma_V\in\mathbf I_n(E)$, $\partial T\Gamma_V=0$, and $\pi_\# T\Gamma_V=\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket$; in particular, $T\Gamma_V\in\mathcal S$.

choices.label: B
choices.text: $T\Gamma_V\in\mathbf I_n(E)$ and $\pi_\#T\Gamma_V=\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket$, but in general one only has $\partial T\Gamma_V=(s_V)_\#\partial\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket$ (so $\partial T\Gamma_V$ need not vanish unless one separately assumes $\partial\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket=0$).

choices.label: C
choices.text: $T\Gamma_V\in\mathbf I_n(E)$ and $\pi_\# T\Gamma_V=\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket$ (hence $T\Gamma_V\in\mathcal S$).

choices.label: D
choices.text: $T\Gamma_V\in\mathbf I_n(E)$, $\partial T\Gamma_V=0$, and $\pi_\# T\Gamma_V=\deg(s_V)\,\llbracket \mathbb S^n\rrbracket$ (so the projection agrees with the fundamental class only up to the integer degree of the section).

choices.label: E
choices.text: $T\Gamma_V\in\mathbf I_n(E)$, $\partial T\Gamma_V=0$, and $\pi_\# T\Gamma_V=0$ in $\mathbf I_n(\mathbb S^n)$, since $\pi\circ s_V=\mathrm{Id}_{\mathbb S^n}$ implies $\pi^*\eta$ is exact on $\Gamma_V$ for every $\eta\in\Omega^n(\mathbb S^n)$.

sketch_usage_meta.label: C

sketch_usage_meta.label: D

ALS.justification: The stem only defines the objects (unit tangent bundle, section, pushforward current) and asks for the strongest provable statement. It does not state or strongly hint that the boundary vanishes or that the projection pushforward equals the fundamental class, beyond the factual identity π∘sV = Id which still requires using pushforward functoriality.

TAS.justification: It is not a mere restatement of a single theorem; the student must combine multiple properties of pushforwards of integral currents (integrality, boundary behavior, projection pushforward) and decide which conclusions really follow under the given assumptions.

GPS.justification: To pick the strongest correct option, one must reason that (i) a smooth map pushes forward the fundamental current to an integral current, (ii) ∂(sV)#⟦Sn⟧ = (sV)#∂⟦Sn⟧ and that ∂⟦Sn⟧ = 0 for the closed manifold Sn, and (iii) π#(sV)# = (π∘sV)# = Id# gives π#TΓV = ⟦Sn⟧. The distractors target precisely these reasoning steps.

DQS.justification: Distractors are plausible and reflect common failure modes: B feigns uncertainty about whether ∂⟦Sn⟧=0; C is a believable weaker-true option; D confuses the degree of a map with the identity π∘sV; E misuses pullback/exactness to force a zero pushforward. They are distinct and tightly aligned with the relevant concepts.

qa quality eval.overall_assessment: High-quality MCQ: no meaningful answer leakage, non-tautological, and it strongly tests generative reasoning about pushforward currents (integrality, boundary, and projection functoriality) with well-crafted distractors, including a weaker-true option.

\label{main thm}
   Let $M^\epsilon \leq M_2 \leq M_1^{1+\epsilon}$.  
   Then  we have 
   \[ \mathcal{S}_\pi(M) \ll_\pi M_1M^\epsilon .\]
theorem.label: main thm

post_theorem_intro_text: The above theorem yields a Lindel\"of consistent bound in the range $ M_2 \asymp M_1$.  Our result extend \cite{D11}  in  the shorter range $ |\mathrm{family}| \asymp M_1^2M_2$. The case $M_2 \geq M_1^{1+\epsilon}$ turns out to be out of reach at the moment as the size of family gets shorter which makes this super hard to analyze from analytic point of view. A key ingredient in the proof is the large sieve inequality which we prove in Lemma \ref{hybrid large-sieve with level}.

mcq.question:
Let $\epsilon>0$ and suppose the parameters $M,M_1,M_2$ satisfy
\[
M^\epsilon \leq M_2 \leq M_1^{1+\epsilon}.
\]
What is the strongest statement that can be proved about $\mathcal{S}_\pi(M)$ under these assumptions (with implied constants allowed to depend on $\pi$)?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text:
One has the bound
\[
\mathcal{S}_\pi(M) \ll_{\pi} M_1\,M^\epsilon.
\]

choices.label: B
choices.text:
One has the bound
\[
\mathcal{S}_\pi(M) \ll_{\pi} (M_1M_2)\,M^\epsilon.
\]

choices.label: C
choices.text:
One has the bound
\[
\mathcal{S}_\pi(M) \ll_{\pi} M_1\,M^{\epsilon}.
\]
In particular, \(\mathcal{S}_\pi(M)=O_{\pi}(M_1M^{\delta})\) for some (unspecified) \(\delta>0\).

choices.label: D
choices.text:
One has the bound
\[
\mathcal{S}_\pi(M) \ll_{\pi,\epsilon} M_1.
\]

choices.label: E
choices.text:
One has the bound
\[
\mathcal{S}_\pi(M) \ll_{\pi} M_2\,M^{\epsilon}.
\]

sketch_usage_meta.label: C
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: dropped the explicit \(\epsilon\)-management (keeps the same main term but weakens by allowing an unspecified positive power of \(M\))

sketch_usage_meta.label: D

sketch_usage_meta.label: E

ALS.justification: Choice A and choice C are textually identical in the main bound (both state S_pi(M) \ll_pi M_1 M^\epsilon), so the correct answer is effectively duplicated among the options. This leaks that the intended bound is exactly that expression, even if C adds a weaker corollary.

TAS.justification: The stem asks for the strongest provable bound under parameter constraints rather than restating a named theorem verbatim; it requires selecting among competing asymptotic dependences (M1 vs M2 vs M1M2, and presence/absence of M^\epsilon).

GPS.justification: In principle it tests judgment about which parameter controls the bound and whether an M^\epsilon loss is unavoidable, but the duplicated correct statement (A/C) makes the reasoning pressure weaker because two options point to the same conclusion.

DQS.justification: Some distractors reflect common failure modes (adding an extra M2 factor; claiming \ll M1 without M^\epsilon; swapping control to M2). However, having C repeat A’s bound makes the set non-distinct and undermines distractor quality/diagnosticity.

qa quality eval.overall_assessment: Conceptually a reasonable 'strongest bound under constraints' question with plausible traps, but it has major answer leakage/structure issues because an incorrect option (C) states the same main bound as the correct option (A), making the MCQ internally inconsistent and reducing its ability to test genuine reasoning.

theorem.content:
\label{main}
Let $H$ be a split classical group over $F$, 
and let $\phi \in \Phi_\mathrm{temp}(H(F))$. 
Suppose that one of the following holds: 
\begin{description}
\item[(B)]
$H = \SO_{2n+1}$, $p > 6n+3$ and $\phi$ is arbitrary; 
\item[(C)]
$H = \Sp_{2n}$, $p > 6n$ and $\phi$ satisfies $(\star)$; 
\item[(D)]
$H = \SO_{2n}$, $p > 6n$ and $\phi$ satisfies $(\star)$. 
\end{description}
Set $\psi = \widehat\phi$. 

\begin{enumerate}
\item
There exists $\pi \in \Pi_\psi$ such that 
\[
d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi) \in \bar\mathcal{N}(\pi)^{\max}.
\]
\item
For $\pi \in \Pi_\psi$ and for $\oo_H^\mathrm{st} \in \bar\mathcal{N}(\pi)$, 
if $\oo_H^\mathrm{st} \not= d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)$, then 
\[
\dim(\oo_H^\mathrm{st}) < \dim(d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)).
\]
Here, $\dim(\oo_H^\mathrm{st})$ is the Zariski dimension of the orbit as an algebraic variety.
\item
If we further assume Hypothesis \ref{hypo} below, then Conjecture \ref{upper} is true for $\phi$, i.e., 
\[
\bar\mathcal{N}(\pi)^{\max} \leq d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)
\]
for any $\pi \in \Pi_\psi$.
\end{enumerate}
theorem.label: main

\[
\sum_{\oo_G \subset \oo_G^\st} a_{\oo_G} \hat\mu_{\oo_G}
\quad\text{is equal to the transfer of}\quad
\sum_{\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st} c_{\oo_H} \hat\mu_{\oo_H}

on a small enough neighborhood of $\theta \in G(F) \rtimes \theta$.
\end{hyp}

\begin{thm}\label{twist}
Let $\phi \colon W_F \times \SL_2(\C) \rightarrow G^\vee$ 
be a self-dual tempered $L$-parameter for $G(F) = \GL_m(F)$, 
and let $\pi_\psi$ be the Zelevinsky dual of the irreducible tempered representation

\bar\NN_\theta(\tl\pi_\psi)^{\max} = \{d_{G^\vee}(\Ad(G^\vee) N_\phi)\}.

for any rational orbits $\oo_G$ and $\oo_G'$ contained in $d_{G^\vee}(\Ad(G^\vee) N_\phi)$.

ref_dict.transfer:
\begin{thm}\label{transfer}
Let $\oo_H^\st \in \NN(\h(\overline{F}))$ be a special nilpotent orbit.
Define $\oo_G^\st \in \NN(\g^\theta(\overline{F}))$ by 
\[
\oo_G^\st = d_{G^\vee}(\Ad(G^\vee)d_{H}(\oo_H^\st)). 
\]
Then for each rational orbit $\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st$, 
there exists a constant $\gamma_{\oo_H} \in \C$ such that 
\[
\sum_{\oo_G \subset \oo_G^\st} \hat\mu_{\oo_G}
\quad\text{is equal to the transfer of }\quad
\sum_{\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st} \gamma_{\oo_H} \hat\mu_{\oo_H}
\]
on a small enough neighborhood of $\theta \in G(F) \rtimes \theta$.
\end{thm}
ref_dict.upper:
\begin{conj}\label{upper}
Let $\phi \in \Phi(H(F))$. 
Then for any $\pi \in \Pi_\phi$, we have
\[
\bar\NN(\hat\pi)^{\max} \leq d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi).
\]
Moreover, if $\phi$ is tempered, 
then the equality holds for some $\pi \in \Pi_\phi$. 
\end{conj}

post_theorem_intro_text:
\subsection{Outline of the proof}\label{sec.outline}
Throughout the paper, we assume that $p \gg 0$ as in Theorem \ref{main}.
The proof of Theorem \ref{main} is similar to the proofs of the Generic Packet Conjecture 
by Konno \cite{K} and Varma \cite{V}. 
The main idea is to compare local character expansions via 
\emph{endoscopic character identities}.
\par

Fix $\phi \in \Phi_\mathrm{temp}(H(F))$ and set $\psi = \widehat\phi$. 
Set $G = \GL_m$, where $m$ is the dimension of the standard representation $H^\vee \rightarrow G^\vee = \GL_m(\mathbb{C})$.
By composing with this map, we can regard $\psi$ as an $A$-parameter for $G(F)$, 
and obtain an irreducible self-dual representation $\pi_\psi$ of $G(F)$. 
Define an involution $\theta$ on $G(F)$ by 
\[
\theta(g) = J{}^tg^{-1}J^{-1}, 
\quad
J = \begin{pmatrix}
&&&1 \\
&&-1&\\
&\iddots&& \\
(-1)^{m-1}&&
\end{pmatrix} \in G(F).
\]
We can extend $\pi_\psi$ to an irreducible representation $\tl\pi_\psi$ of $G \rtimes \langle \theta \rangle$.
The twisted character of $\tl\pi_\psi$ is denoted by $\Theta_{\tl\pi_\psi}$. 
\par

Let $\Sc_\psi$ be the component group for $\psi$, 
and let $\widehat\Sc_\psi$ be its Pontryagin dual. 
Recall that Arthur defined a map
\[
\Pi_\psi \rightarrow \widehat\Sc_\psi, \;
\pi \mapsto \langle \cdot, \pi \rangle_\psi. 
\]
Notice that this is bijective since $\psi = \widehat\phi$.
Set $s_\psi = \psi(\1_{W_F}, \mathbf{1}, -\mathbf{1}) = \phi(\1_{W_F}, -\mathbf{1})$.
In this setting, \cite[Theorem 2.2.1]{Ar} asserts that 
\begin{description}
\item[(T1)]
the distribution
\[
S\Theta_{\psi} = \sum_{\pi \in \Pi_\psi} \langle s_\psi, \pi \rangle_\psi \Theta_\pi
\]
is stable, and $\Theta_{\tl\pi_\psi}$ is the transfer of $S\Theta_\psi$; 
\item[(T2)]
Each $s \in \Sc_\psi$ with $s \not= 1$ gives an elliptic endoscopic group $H_1 \times H_2$ of $H$
and an $A$-parameter $\psi_i$ for $H_i$ 
(of the form $\psi_i = \widehat\phi_i$ for some $\phi_i \in \Phi_\mathrm{temp}(H_i)$) such that 
\[
S\Theta_{\psi, s} = \sum_{\pi \in \Pi_\psi} \langle s \cdot s_\psi, \pi \rangle_\psi \Theta_\pi
\]
is the transfer of $S\Theta_{\psi_1} \otimes S\Theta_{\psi_2}$. 
\end{description}
\par

The first step of the proof of Theorem \ref{main} is to establish an analogue for the twisted $\GL_m$ case.
By the twisted local character expansion established by Clozel \cite[Theorem 3]{C}, 
we can expand
\[
\Theta_{\tl\pi_\psi} 
= \sum_{\oo_G \in \mathcal{N}(\mathfrak{g}^\theta(F))} c_{\oo_G}(\tl\pi_\psi) \hat\mu_{\oo_G}. 
\]
See Section \ref{sec.TLCE} below for the notations. 
We define $\NN_\theta(\tl\pi_\psi) \subset \mathcal{N}(\mathfrak{g}^\theta(F))$ 
and $\bar\NN_\theta(\tl\pi_\psi) \subset \mathcal{N}(\mathfrak{g}^\theta(\overline{F}))$
similar to $\mathcal{N}(\pi)$ and $\bar\mathcal{N}(\pi)$, respectively. 
In Theorem \ref{twist} below, we will show that 
\[
\bar\NN_\theta(\tl\pi_\psi)^{\max} = \{d_{G^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(G^\vee) N_\phi)\}.
\]
This is an immediate consequence of 
results of Konno \cite{K}, Varma \cite{V}, and M{\oe}glin--Waldspurger \cite{MW}.
Moreover, Konno's result \cite[Theorem 4.1(2)]{K} says that  
the constant $c_{\oo_G}(\tl\pi_\psi)$ for $\oo_G \subset d_{G^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(G^\vee) N_\phi)$ 
does not depend on the choice of the rational orbit.
\par

Set $\oo_H^\mathrm{st} = d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee) N_\phi)$ and $\oo_G^\mathrm{st} = d_{G^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(G^\vee) N_\phi)$.
The second step of the proof of Theorem \ref{main} is to show that 
there exists a constant $\gamma_{\oo_H}$ for each rational orbit $\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\mathrm{st}$ such that 
\[
\sum_{\oo_G \subset \oo_G^\mathrm{st}} \hat\mu_{\oo_G}
\quad
\text{is equal to the transfer of} 
\quad
\sum_{\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\mathrm{st}} \gamma_{\oo_H}\hat\mu_{\oo_H}
\]
on a small enough neighborhood of $\theta \in G(F) \rtimes \theta$.
See Theorem \ref{transfer} below. 
Hypothesis \ref{hypo} is an analogue of this result. 
These claims could be proven by similar arguments to the standard case explained in the next paragraph, 
but there is no explicit reference in the literature.
Thus we will prove Theorem \ref{transfer} in this paper. 
The proof uses Conjecture \ref{upper} in the case established in \cite{CMBO2},
which requires that $H$ is split over $F$.
\par

An analogous result for the standard endoscopy with unramified endoscopic groups
is known by Waldspurger \cite{W_pave}. 
Let $H_1 \times H_2$ be an unramified endoscopic group of $H$. 
For a special nilpotent orbit $\oo_{H_i}^\mathrm{st} \in \mathcal{N}(\h_i(\overline{F}))$, 
Waldspurger explicitly defined a nilpotent orbit
\[
\oo_H^\mathrm{st} = W(\oo_{H_1}^\mathrm{st}, \oo_{H_2}^\mathrm{st}) \in \mathcal{N}(\mathfrak{h}(\overline{F})),
\]
and proved a certain transfer result in \cite[XII.9 Th\'eor\`eme]{W_pave}.
The third step of the proof of Theorem \ref{main} is to relate the Waldspurger map $W(\oo_{H_1}^\mathrm{st}, \oo_{H_2}^\mathrm{st})$
and the Spaltenstein duality (Proposition \ref{WS}). 
\par

Combining the two transfer results, we can relate the local character expansion of $S\Theta_\psi$ (resp.~ $S\Theta_{\psi,s}$)
with the one of $\Theta_{\tl\pi_\psi}$ (resp.~ $S\Theta_{\psi_1} \otimes S\Theta_{\psi_2}$).
Then by induction on $m$, 
we can deduce Theorem \ref{main} in Section \ref{sec.proof}. 
To use \cite[XII.9 Th\'eor\`eme]{W_pave}, we need the condition ($\star$) in Cases (C) and (D), 
which is equivalent to saying that all endoscopic groups $H_1 \times H_2$ arising from $s \in \Sc_\psi$ are unramified. 

\begin{rem}\label{OvsSO}
The local Langlands correspondence for $H = \SO_{2n}$ as proven by Arthur, 
is given up to $\O_{2n}(F)$-conjugation. 
Thus, in turn, we should replace $\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi$ by $\mathrm{Ad}(\O_{2n}(\mathbb{C}))N_\phi$ in our results. 
We will ignore this discrepancy since it is not an important difference for the geometric wavefront set results.
By replacing $\SO_{2n}$ with $\O_{2n}$, we can use the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
the distributions on $\SO_{2n}(F)$ considered in the paper are all $\O_{2n}(F)$-invariant;
\item
the transfer of stable distributions on $H(F)$ to $G(F) \rtimes \theta$ is injective;
\item
$\mathrm{Ad}(G^\vee)\oo_{H^\vee} \cap H^\vee = \oo_{H^\vee}$ for $\oo_{H^\vee} \in \mathcal{N}(\mathfrak{h}^\vee)$.
\end{enumerate}
Note that (2) and (3) hold when $H = \SO_{2n+1}$ or $H = \Sp_{2n}$. 
\end{rem}

The proof of Theorem \ref{main} is said to be “similar to the proofs of the Generic Packet Conjecture by Konno \cite{K} and Varma \cite{V},” and “the main idea is to compare local character expansions via \emph{endoscopic character identities}.” After fixing $\phi\in\Phi_\mathrm{temp}(H(F))$ and setting $\psi=\widehat\phi$, one embeds into $G=\GL_m$ (via the standard representation $H^\vee\to G^\vee$), views $\psi$ as an $A$-parameter for $G(F)$, and obtains an irreducible self-dual $\pi_\psi$; one then extends it to $\tl\pi_\psi$ on $G\rtimes\langle\theta\rangle$ and uses its twisted character $\Theta_{\tl\pi_\psi}$.

Using Arthur’s identities \cite[Theorem 2.2.1]{Ar}, one has (T1) that
\[
S\Theta_{\psi}=\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_\psi}\langle s_\psi,\pi\rangle_\psi\,\Theta_\pi
\]
“is stable, and $\Theta_{\tl\pi_\psi}$ is the transfer of $S\Theta_\psi$,” and (T2) that for $s\neq 1$ one gets an elliptic endoscopic group $H_1\times H_2$ with parameters $\psi_i=\widehat\phi_i$ such that
\[
S\Theta_{\psi,s}=\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_\psi}\langle s\cdot s_\psi,\pi\rangle_\psi\,\Theta_\pi
\]
“is the transfer of $S\Theta_{\psi_1}\otimes S\Theta_{\psi_2}$.”

The outline is organized into three steps:

1) “The first step” is to prove an analogue on the twisted $\GL_m$ side. Using Clozel’s “twisted local character expansion” one expands
\[
\Theta_{\tl\pi_\psi}=\sum_{\oo_G\in\mathcal N(\mathfrak g^\theta(F))}c_{\oo_G}(\tl\pi_\psi)\,\hat\mu_{\oo_G},
\]
defines the corresponding maximal nilpotent sets $\bar\NN_\theta(\tl\pi_\psi)^{\max}$, and shows (Theorem \ref{twist}) that
\[
\bar\NN_\theta(\tl\pi_\psi)^{\max}=\{d_{G^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(G^\vee)N_\phi)\},
\]
“as an immediate consequence of results of Konno \cite{K}, Varma \cite{V}, and M{\oe}glin--Waldspurger \cite{MW}.” It is also noted (via Konno) that for $\oo_G\subset d_{G^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(G^\vee)N_\phi)$, the constant $c_{\oo_G}(\tl\pi_\psi)$ “does not depend on the choice of the rational orbit.”

2) Writing $\oo_H^\mathrm{st}=d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)$ and $\oo_G^\mathrm{st}=d_{G^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(G^\vee)N_\phi)$, “the second step” proves a transfer statement at the level of nilpotent orbital integrals: there exists $\gamma_{\oo_H}$ for each rational orbit $\oo_H\subset\oo_H^\mathrm{st}$ such that
\[
\sum_{\oo_G\subset\oo_G^\mathrm{st}}\hat\mu_{\oo_G}\quad\text{is equal to the transfer of}\quad\sum_{\oo_H\subset\oo_H^\mathrm{st}}\gamma_{\oo_H}\hat\mu_{\oo_H}
\]
“on a small enough neighborhood of $\theta\in G(F)\rtimes\theta$” (Theorem \ref{transfer} below). Hypothesis \ref{hypo} is described as an analogue of this result.

3) “The third step” uses Waldspurger’s transfer for standard endoscopy with unramified endoscopic groups: for $H_1\times H_2$ and special orbits $\oo_{H_i}^\mathrm{st}$, Waldspurger defines
\[
\oo_H^\mathrm{st}=W(\oo_{H_1}^\mathrm{st},\oo_{H_2}^\mathrm{st})
\]
and proves a transfer theorem; the proof then “relate[s] the Waldspurger map $W(\oo_{H_1}^\mathrm{st},\oo_{H_2}^\mathrm{st})$ and the Spaltenstein duality (Proposition \ref{WS}).”

Finally, “combining the two transfer results,” one relates character expansions of $S\Theta_\psi$ (and $S\Theta_{\psi,s}$) to those of $\Theta_{\tl\pi_\psi}$ (and $S\Theta_{\psi_1}\otimes S\Theta_{\psi_2}$), and “by induction on $m$” deduces Theorem \ref{main}. The outline also notes that to apply Waldspurger’s theorem one needs condition $(\star)$ in Cases (C) and (D), “equivalent to saying that all endoscopic groups $H_1\times H_2$ arising from $s\in\Sc_\psi$ are unramified.”

\[
\Theta_{\tl\pi_\psi}=\sum_{\oo_G\in\mathcal N(\mathfrak g^\theta(F))}c_{\oo_G}(\tl\pi_\psi)\,\hat\mu_{\oo_G},
\]
defines the corresponding maximal nilpotent sets $\bar\NN_\theta(\tl\pi_\psi)^{\max}$, and shows the following theorem.

\begin{thm}\label{twist}
Let $\phi \colon W_F \times \SL_2(\C) \rightarrow G^\vee$ 
be a self-dual tempered $L$-parameter for $G(F) = \GL_m(F)$, 
and let $\pi_\psi$ be the Zelevinsky dual of the irreducible tempered representation 
$\pi_\phi$ corresponding to $\phi$. 
Then 
\[
\bar\NN_\theta(\tl\pi_\psi)^{\max} = \{d_{G^\vee}(\Ad(G^\vee) N_\phi)\}.
\]
Moreover, $c_{\oo_G}(\tl\pi_\psi) = c_{\oo_G'}(\tl\pi_\psi)$ 
for any rational orbits $\oo_G$ and $\oo_G'$ contained in $d_{G^\vee}(\Ad(G^\vee) N_\phi)$.
\end{thm}

This is described as “an immediate consequence of results of Konno \cite{K}, Varma \cite{V}, and M{\oe}glin--Waldspurger \cite{MW}.”

2) Writing $\oo_H^\mathrm{st}=d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)$ and $\oo_G^\mathrm{st}=d_{G^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(G^\vee)N_\phi)$, “the second step” proves a transfer statement at the level of nilpotent orbital integrals, namely the following theorem.

\begin{thm}\label{transfer}
Let $\oo_H^\st \in \NN(\h(\overline{F}))$ be a special nilpotent orbit.
Define $\oo_G^\st \in \NN(\g^\theta(\overline{F}))$ by 
\[
\oo_G^\st = d_{G^\vee}(\Ad(G^\vee)d_{H}(\oo_H^\st)). 
\]
Then for each rational orbit $\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st$, 
there exists a constant $\gamma_{\oo_H} \in \C$ such that 
\[
\sum_{\oo_G \subset \oo_G^\st} \hat\mu_{\oo_G}
\quad\text{is equal to the transfer of }\quad
\sum_{\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st} \gamma_{\oo_H} \hat\mu_{\oo_H}
\]
on a small enough neighborhood of $\theta \in G(F) \rtimes \theta$.
\end{thm}

Hypothesis \ref{hypo} is described as an analogue of this result; explicitly:

\begin{hyp}\label{hypo}
Let $\oo_H^\st \in \NN(\h(\overline{F}))$ be a special nilpotent orbit.

\[
\oo_G^\st = d_{G^\vee}(\Ad(G^\vee)d_{H}(\oo_H^\st)). 
\]
Then for any constants $\{c_{\oo_H} \;|\; \oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st\}$ such that 
$\sum_{\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st} c_{\oo_H} \hat\mu_{\oo_H}$ is stable, 
there exist constants $\{a_{\oo_G} \;|\; \oo_G \subset \oo_G^\st\}$ such that 
\[
\sum_{\oo_G \subset \oo_G^\st} a_{\oo_G} \hat\mu_{\oo_G}
\quad\text{is equal to the transfer of}\quad
\sum_{\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st} c_{\oo_H} \hat\mu_{\oo_H} 
\]
on a small enough neighborhood of $\theta \in G(F) \rtimes \theta$.
\end{hyp}

3) “The third step” uses Waldspurger’s transfer for standard endoscopy with unramified endoscopic groups: for $H_1\times H_2$ and special orbits $\oo_{H_i}^\mathrm{st}$, Waldspurger defines
\[

For $i \in \{1,2\}$, let $\oo_{H_i}^\st \in \NN(\h_i(\overline{F}))$ be a special nilpotent orbit.
Then 
\[
W(\oo_{H_1}^\st, \oo_{H_2}^\st) 
\leq d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)\xi(d_{H_1}(\oo_{H_1}^\st), d_{H_2}(\oo_{H_2}^\st))). 
\]
\end{prop}

Finally, “combining the two transfer results,” one relates character expansions of $S\Theta_\psi$ (and $S\Theta_{\psi,s}$) to those of $\Theta_{\tl\pi_\psi}$ (and $S\Theta_{\psi_1}\otimes S\Theta_{\psi_2}$), and “by induction on $m$” completes the proof of the main theorem. expanded_theorem:
\label{main}
Let $H$ be a split classical group over $F$, 
and let $\phi \in \Phi_\mathrm{temp}(H(F))$. 
Suppose that one of the following holds: 
\begin{description}
\item[(B)]
$H = \SO_{2n+1}$, $p > 6n+3$ and $\phi$ is arbitrary; 
\item[(C)]
$H = \Sp_{2n}$, $p > 6n$ and $\phi$ satisfies $(\star)$; 
\item[(D)]
$H = \SO_{2n}$, $p > 6n$ and $\phi$ satisfies $(\star)$. 
\end{description}
Set $\psi = \widehat\phi$. 

\begin{enumerate}
\item
There exists $\pi \in \Pi_\psi$ such that 
\[
d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi) \in \bar\mathcal{N}(\pi)^{\max}.
\]
\item
For $\pi \in \Pi_\psi$ and for $\oo_H^\mathrm{st} \in \bar\mathcal{N}(\pi)$, 
if $\oo_H^\mathrm{st} \not= d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)$, then 
\[
\dim(\oo_H^\mathrm{st}) < \dim(d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)).
\]
Here, $\dim(\oo_H^\mathrm{st})$ is the Zariski dimension of the orbit as an algebraic variety.
\item
If we further assume the following hypothesis, then the stated upper-bound conjecture holds for $\phi$.

\begin{hyp}\label{hypo}
Let $\oo_H^\st \in \NN(\h(\overline{F}))$ be a special nilpotent orbit.
Define $\oo_G^\st \in \NN(\g^\theta(\overline{F}))$ by 
\[
\oo_G^\st = d_{G^\vee}(\Ad(G^\vee)d_{H}(\oo_H^\st)). 
\]
Then for any constants $\{c_{\oo_H} \;|\; \oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st\}$ such that 
$\sum_{\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st} c_{\oo_H} \hat\mu_{\oo_H}$ is stable, 
there exist constants $\{a_{\oo_G} \;|\; \oo_G \subset \oo_G^\st\}$ such that 
\[
\sum_{\oo_G \subset \oo_G^\st} a_{\oo_G} \hat\mu_{\oo_G}
\quad\text{is equal to the transfer of}\quad
\sum_{\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st} c_{\oo_H} \hat\mu_{\oo_H} 
\]
on a small enough neighborhood of $\theta \in G(F) \rtimes \theta$.
\end{hyp}

We first record the conjecture in question.
\begin{conj}\label{upper}
Let $\phi \in \Phi(H(F))$. 
Then for any $\pi \in \Pi_\phi$, we have
\[
\bar\NN(\hat\pi)^{\max} \leq d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi).
\]
Moreover, if $\phi$ is tempered, 
then the equality holds for some $\pi \in \Pi_\phi$. 
\end{conj}

In particular,
\[
\bar\mathcal{N}(\pi)^{\max} \leq d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)
\]
for any $\pi \in \Pi_\psi$.
\end{enumerate}

mcq.question:
Let \(\mathrm{d}'\) be a differential operator acting on smooth sections so that for each \(q\) there is a map
\[
\mathrm{d}': \mathscr{C}^\infty(G;\underline{\Lambda}^{q-1}) \to \mathscr{C}^\infty(G;\underline{\Lambda}^{q}),
\]
and set \(n \doteq \operatorname{rank}(\mathcal{V})\). Assume that
\[
\mathrm{d}': \mathscr{C}^\infty(G) \longrightarrow \mathscr{C}^\infty(G;\underline{\Lambda}^{1})
\quad \text{has closed range}.
\]
Define \(\mathscr{K}(G)\subset \mathscr{C}^\infty(G)\) by: \(f\in\mathscr{K}(G)\) iff \(\mathrm{L}f=0\) for every smooth section \(\mathrm{L}\) of \(\mathcal{V}\). Let \(H^q_{\mathrm{d}'}(\mathscr{C}^\infty(G))\) be the \(\mathrm{d}'\)-cohomology, and let \(H^q_{\mathrm{d}'}(\mathbb{C}_G)\) denote the space of left-invariant classes in \(H^q_{\mathrm{d}'}(\mathscr{C}^\infty(G))\) (with \(\mathbb{C}_G\) the constant functions on \(G\)).

Which of the following is the strongest consequence of these assumptions?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text:
For every \(q\) with \(1\le q\le n\), the map \(\mathrm{d}':\mathscr{C}^\infty(G;\underline{\Lambda}^{q-1})\to \mathscr{C}^\infty(G;\underline{\Lambda}^{q})\) has closed range. Moreover, for each \(0\le q\le n\) there is a topological isomorphism
\[
H^{q}_{\mathrm{d}'} (\mathscr{C}^\infty(G)) \cong \mathscr{K}(G) \otimes H^{q}_{\mathrm{d}'} (\mathbb{C}_G).
\]

choices.label: B
choices.text:
For every \(q\) with \(1\le q\le n\), the map \(\mathrm{d}':\mathscr{C}^\infty(G;\underline{\Lambda}^{q-1})\to \mathscr{C}^\infty(G;\underline{\Lambda}^{q})\) has closed range. Moreover, for each \(0\le q\le n\) there is a (non-canonical) \emph{algebraic} vector-space isomorphism
\[
H^{q}_{\mathrm{d}'} (\mathscr{C}^\infty(G)) \cong \mathscr{K}(G) \otimes H^{q}_{\mathrm{d}'} (\mathbb{C}_G),
\]
without any claim that it is a topological isomorphism.

choices.label: C
choices.text: For every \(q\) with \(1\le q\le n\), the map \(\mathrm{d}':\mathscr{C}^\infty(G;\underline{\Lambda}^{q-1})\to \mathscr{C}^\infty(G;\underline{\Lambda}^{q})\) has closed range.

choices.label: D
choices.text:
For every \(q\) with \(1\le q\le n\), the map \(\mathrm{d}':\mathscr{C}^\infty(G;\underline{\Lambda}^{q-1})\to \mathscr{C}^\infty(G;\underline{\Lambda}^{q})\) has closed range. Moreover, for each \(0\le q\le n\) there is a topological isomorphism
\[
H^{q}_{\mathrm{d}'} (\mathscr{C}^\infty(G)) \cong H^{q}_{\mathrm{d}'}(\mathscr{K}(G)),
\]
and in particular \(H^{q}_{\mathrm{d}'}(\mathscr{C}^\infty(G))\) is finite-dimensional for all \(q\).

choices.label: E
choices.text:
For every \(q\) with \(1\le q\le n\), the map \(\mathrm{d}':\mathscr{C}^\infty(G;\underline{\Lambda}^{q-1})\to \mathscr{C}^\infty(G;\underline{\Lambda}^{q})\) has closed range. Moreover, for each \(0\le q\le n\) there is a topological isomorphism
\[
H^{q}_{\mathrm{d}'} (\mathscr{C}^\infty(G)) \cong \mathscr{K}(G) \otimes H^{q}_{\mathrm{d}'} (\mathbb{C}_G),
\]
and in addition \(H^{q}_{\mathrm{d}'} (\mathbb{C}_G)=0\) for all \(1\le q\le n\).

mcq.question:
Let $1\leq p<2$ and $d\geq 1$. Assume the pressure law $P$ satisfies $P'(\bar{\rho})>0$ for $\bar{\rho}>0$. Suppose there exists a sufficiently small constant $\delta_1>0$ such that the initial data $(n_0,\mathbf{v}_0)$ satisfy
\[
\|(n_0,\mathbf{v}_0)\|_{\dot{B}_{p,1}^{\frac{d}{p}}}^{\ell,J_\varepsilon}
+\varepsilon\,(\|(n_0,\mathbf{v}_0)\|_{\dot{B}_{2,1}^{\frac{d}{2}+1}}^{h,J_\varepsilon})
\leq \delta_1.
\]
Consider, for $\varepsilon>0$, the Cauchy problem
\[
\left\{\begin{aligned}
&\partial_t n + \mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla n + P'(\bar{\rho})\,\operatorname{div}\mathbf{v} + G(n)\,\operatorname{div}\mathbf{v} = 0,\\
&\partial_t \mathbf{v}+ \mathbf{v}\cdot \nabla \mathbf{v}+\nabla n= -\frac{1}{\varepsilon} \mathbf{v},
\end{aligned}\right.
\qquad (n,\mathbf{v})\big|_{t=0}=(n_0,\mathbf{v}_0).
\]
What is the strongest statement that can be proved about solutions to this Cauchy problem under the assumptions above?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: For every $\varepsilon>0$, the above Cauchy problem admits a uniform global (in time) unique solution $(n,\mathbf{v})$ belonging to the space $E_\infty^{J_\varepsilon}$.

choices.label: B
choices.text: There exists $ ar\varepsilon>0$ such that for every $\varepsilon\in(0,\bar\varepsilon]$, the above Cauchy problem admits a global unique solution $(n,\mathbf{v})\in E_\infty^{J_\varepsilon}$, and the corresponding a priori bounds are uniform with respect to $\varepsilon$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: For every $\varepsilon>0$, the above Cauchy problem admits a (possibly non-uniform) global (in time) unique solution $(n,\mathbf{v})$ belonging to the space $E_\infty^{J_\varepsilon}$.

choices.label: D
choices.text:
For every $\varepsilon>0$, the above Cauchy problem admits a uniform global unique solution $(n,\mathbf{v})\in E_\infty^{J_\varepsilon}$ provided the smallness condition is strengthened to
\[
\|(n_0,\mathbf{v}_0)\|_{\dot B_{p,1}^{\frac{d}{p}}}^{\ell,J_\varepsilon}+\|(n_0,\mathbf{v}_0)\|_{\dot B_{2,1}^{\frac{d}{2}+1}}^{h,J_\varepsilon}\le \delta_1,
\]
i.e. without the factor $\varepsilon$ in front of the high-frequency term.

choices.label: E
choices.text:
There exists a small constant $\delta_1>0$ such that if
\[
\|(n_0,\mathbf{v}_0)\|_{\dot{B}_{p,1}^{\frac{d}{p}}}^{\ell,J_\varepsilon}+\varepsilon\,(\|(n_0,\mathbf{v}_0)\|_{\dot{B}_{2,1}^{\frac{d}{2}+1}}^{h,J_\varepsilon})\le\delta_1,
\]
then for every $\varepsilon>0$ the Cauchy problem admits a uniform global weak solution $(n,\mathbf{v})\in L^\infty(\mathbb R_+;\dot B_{p,1}^{\frac{d}{p}})\times L^\infty(\mathbb R_+;\dot B_{p,1}^{\frac{d}{p}-1})$ (not necessarily unique) satisfying the equations in the sense of distributions.

theorem.content:
Let $1<p<\infty$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^N$ be an open set. Let us suppose that there exists $k\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}$ such that
\begin{equation}\
\label{PL}
\lambda_{k,p}^{\rm LS}(\Omega)<\mathcal{E}_p(\Omega).
\end{equation}
Then, for every $\ell\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ the minmax value $\lambda_{\ell,p}^{\rm LS}(\Omega)$ is an eigenvalue of the Dirichlet $p-$Laplacian on $\Omega$. 
\par
Moreover, we have:
\begin{itemize}
\item if $\mathcal{E}_p(\Omega)<+\infty$,  for every $\ell\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ there exist two constants $C_\ell=C_\ell(N, p, \Omega)>0$ and $\alpha_\ell=\alpha_\ell(p,\Omega)>0$ such that for every eigenfunction $u_\ell\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ associated to $\lambda_{\ell,p}^{\rm LS}(\Omega)$, we have
\[
|u_\ell(x)|\le C_\ell\,\|u_\ell\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\,e^{-\alpha_\ell\,|x|}\,,\qquad \text{for every}\ x\in\Omega;
\]
\item if $\mathcal{E}_p(\Omega)=+\infty$, for every $\ell\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}$ and every $\alpha>0$ there exists a constant $C_\ell=C_\ell(N, p,\Omega,\alpha)>0$ such that 
\[
|u_\ell(x)|\le C_\ell\,\|u_\ell\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\,e^{-\alpha\,|x|}\,,\qquad \text{for every}\ x\in\Omega.
\]
\end{itemize}
theorem.label: PL

ref_dict.defi:scp:
\begin{defi}
\label{defi:scp}
Let $V\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^N)$ be a non-negative function. We say that $V$ is a {\it strongly confining potential} if it has the following property: there exists an increasing function $\alpha:(0,+\infty)\to(0,+\infty)$ such that
\[
\lim_{R\to +\infty} \alpha(R)=+\infty,
\]
and for every $R>0$ we have
\[
V(x)\ge \alpha(R),\qquad \text{for a.e.}\ x\in \mathbb{R}^N\setminus B_R.
\]
\end{defi}
ref_dict.lm:giggi:
\begin{lm}
\label{lm:giggi}
Let $1<p<\infty$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^N$ be an open set such that $\lambda_{1,p}(\Omega)>0$. Let $X(\Omega)$ be a Banach space with the following properties:
\begin{itemize}
\item $C^\infty_0(\Omega)\subseteq X(\Omega)$;
\vskip.2cm
\item $X(\Omega)\subseteq W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ with continuous inclusion, i.e. there exists $C>0$ such that
\[
\|\nabla \varphi\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C\, \|\varphi\|_{X(\Omega)},\qquad \text{for every}\ \varphi\in X(\Omega).
\]
\end{itemize}
We set
\[
\mathcal{X}_{k,p}(\Omega)=\Big\{K\subseteq \mathcal{S}_p(\Omega)\cap X(\Omega)\, :\, K\ \text{symmetric and compact},\, \gamma(K;X(\Omega))\ge k\Big\},
\]
and
\[
\mathcal{W}_{k,p}(\Omega)=\Big\{K\subseteq \mathcal{S}_p(\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)\, :\, K\ \text{symmetric and compact},\, \gamma(K;W^{1,p}_0(\Omega))\ge k\Big\}.
\]
Then, for every $K\in \mathcal{W}_{k,p}(\Omega)$ and every $\delta>0$, there exists $K_\delta\in \mathcal{X}_{k,p}(\Omega)$ such that
\[
\max_{\varphi\in K_\delta} \int_\Omega |\nabla \varphi|^p\,dx\le \max_{\varphi\in K} \int_\Omega |\nabla \varphi|^p\,dx+\delta.
\]
\end{lm}

post_theorem_intro_text:
The rest of this subsection is devoted to a couple of (detailed) comments on this result. We start with the exponential fall-off.
\begin{rem}[Fall-off]
\label{rem:SS}
As for the ``compact case'' $\mathcal{E}_p(\Omega)=+\infty$, our decay estimate represents an extension to the nonlinear case of \cite[Theorem 2]{Si2} by Simon, recalled above. The latter deals with Schr\"odinger operators $-\Delta+V$ on the whole $\mathbb{R}^N$, under the effect of a non-negative strongly confining potential $V$ (see Definition \ref{defi:scp} below).
\par
In the ``non-compact case'' $\mathcal{E}_p(\Omega)<+\infty$, our estimate is a nonlinear variation on the classical result by \v{S}nol, previously recalled. In particular, we have that
\[
\alpha_k\le \dots\le \alpha_1,
\]
with the notation above.
That is, the higher the eigenvalue, the slower the exponential decay. Moreover, these exponents deteriorate (i.e. they approach $0$) as the eigenvalues approach the spectral threshold $\mathcal{E}_p(\Omega)$: we refer to Proposition \ref{prop:lambdadecay} below, for this fact. 
This behaviour is in perfect accordance with \v{S}nol's result.
Indeed, in \cite[Theorem pag. 282]{Sn}, this estimate is proved for eigenfunctions of $-\Delta+V$, corresponding to an eigenvalue $\lambda$ below of the essential spectrum $\mathcal{E}_V$. Also in \cite{Sn}, the exponent $\alpha$ dictating the fall-off depends on the difference $\mathcal{E}_V-\lambda$ and it goes to $0$, as this difference goes to $0$. More precisely, \v{S}nol's exponent is given by 
\[
\alpha=\log\left(1+\frac{\mathcal{E}_V-\lambda}{K}\right),
\]
for constant $K$ depending on the (positive) potential $V$.
 For these reasons, in what follows we will refer to the estimate of the Main Theorem as {\it \v{S}nol-Simon--type decay estimate}.
\par
Finally, we wish to point out that our method of proof is different from those of both \cite{Si2} and \cite{Sn} and based on nonlinear techniques: we first obtain exponential decay in $L^p$ norm and then use an $L^\infty-L^p$ estimate ``localized at infinity'' to transform it into a pointwise decay estimate. The decay in $L^p$ norm is obtained by combining Caccioppoli and Poincar\'e inequalities, while the second estimate is a classical tool in the De Giorgi-Moser regularity theory for quasilinear equations.
\par 
It is worth mentioning that, once we obtain decay estimates on the eigenfunctions, it is possible to exploit the equation so to obtain some decay and integrability estimates on their gradients, as well (see Corollary \ref{coro:gradienti} below).
\end{rem}
We then briefly comment on how we prove the existence part of the Main Theorem.
\begin{rem}[Existence of eigenfunctions]
There are various ways to get existence of eigenfunctions. Of course, we can focus on the case $\mathcal{E}_p(\Omega)<+\infty$, in light of what we have previously recalled. In the Hilbertian setting (i.\,e. for $p=2$), a purely variational approach based on concentration-compactness arguments is provided by Smets, see \cite[Theorem 4.1 $\&$ Theorem 4.2]{Sm}, for a slightly different eigenvalue problem. His approach relies on the possibility to characterize higher eigenvalues as an infimum, possibly on the orthogonal complement of a finite dimensional vector space. This fact is true for $p=2$, but it has no counterpart for $p \neq 2$. For this reason, it is less clear whether this approach can be applied for the full range of $p$, see for instance \cite[Remark 4.4 (b)]{Sm}. 
\par
We briefly explain our route. We use a {\it spectral stability argument}, i.e. we prove that our minmax Ljusternik-Schnirelmann values can be approximated by the eigenvalues of a perturbed operator, having good compactness properties.
More precisely, we ``compactify'' the original eigenvalue problem by considering a new family of problems, each one obtained by adding a strongly confining potential $V_n$. For this family, we can prove existence of infinitely many ``perturbed'' eigenvalues, by the usual minmax procedure recalled above. Moreover, if $V_n$ tends to $0$ (in a suitable sense) as $n$ goes to $\infty$, we can prove that these eigenvalues converge to the original minmax Ljusternik-Schnirelmann values. Then, in order to prove that those lying below $\mathcal{E}_p(\Omega)$ actually define an eigenvalue, we aim to infer strong convergence in $L^p$ of the ``perturbed'' eigenfunctions. Here, we crucially exploit that these ``perturbed'' eigenfunctions enjoy a uniform \v{S}nol-Simon decay estimate, whenever they are associated to a ``perturbed'' eigenvalue which is converging to a $\lambda_{k,p}^{\rm LS}(\Omega)<\mathcal{E}_p(\Omega)$. The uniform fall-off in turn implies an $L^p$ equi-tightness property, which permits to appeal to the classical Riesz-Fr\'echet-Kolmogorov compactness criterion. In a nutshell, we obtain compactness through regularity. 
\par
In the language of Calculus of Variations, this is essentially a $\Gamma-$convergence--type argument in disguise, but used for higher critical points, other than the global minimum (see \cite{Brai,Dal} for the general theory of $\Gamma-$convergence). In doing this, we crucially borrow some ideas from the paper \cite{CD} by Champion and De Pascale.
\end{rem}

\subsection{Plan of the paper}
The paper starts with some preliminary materials contained in Section \ref{sec:2}. The main content of Section \ref{sec:3} is the \v{S}nol-Simon--type estimate of Proposition \ref{prop:lambdadecay}, which holds more generally for non-negative {\it subsolutions} of the eigenvalue equation. As a consequence, we also obtain some decay and integrability properties for their gradients. Section \ref{sec:4} is devoted to the ``perturbed'' eigenvalue problem described above, obtained by adding a strongly confining potential. Here, the technical Lemma \ref{lm:giggi} may be of some independent interest. The proof of the Main Theorem is contained in Section \ref{sec:5}, while in Section \ref{sec:6} we provide some examples of unbounded open sets to which our result applies. The paper ends with two appendices: in particular, in Appendix \ref{sec:B} we show that, for $p=2$, the minmax Ljusternik-Schnirelmann values below the essential spectrum coincide with the eigenvalues given by the Courant-Fischer formula.

Assume that $0\le u\le 1$ is a  stable radial solution to \eqref{d-p}.
If $2\le n\le 6$, then $u$ is regular and satisfies
$$\frac 12 u_r(1)^2\le F(\|u\|_{L^\infty(B_1)})\le  Cu_r(1)^2.$$
Additionally, if $f$ is nondecreasing, then
 $$F(\|u\|_{L^\infty(B_1)})\le C,$$
where  $C>0$ is a universal constant.
